title: Chapter 2 | How We Learned How We Learn
text: CHAPTER 2 How We Learned How We Learn For forty-two years, Henry Molaison carried a note in his pocket that simply read, “Dad’s dead.” 8 In one conversation, he said, “I am having a debate with myself—about my dad … I’m not easy in my mind. On the one side, I think he has been called—he’s gone—but on the other, I think he’s alive.” You see, following a brain surgery, Henry’s brain could not make new memories. He lived with his parents, and after his father died, he would periodically search the house for his father, only to be told his father had died and to reexperience the initial grief all over again. Studying his brain was critical to the advances in our learning about how we learn. It was 1953. Henry was just twenty-seven years old and suffering from severe epileptic seizures when his medical team decided on an experimental surgery to remove a section of his brain, including a part called the hippocampus, with unforeseen consequences. 9 Henry lived for fifty-five more years and never made a new memory because his brain’s ability to learn had unintentionally been turned off. The Most Studied Brain in Human History Henry provided us with the most studied brain in human history. He once said that while he did not really understand all that was happening to him because he had no memory of the thousands of interviews and brain imaging sessions, he believed that people were good, and his hope was that his brain might help people in the future in some way. He was, by all accounts, a lovely and kind man. We would learn a great deal indeed from Henry Molaison and his tragedy. He taught us, as a species, that all new learning, with the exception of some motor skills, passes through, and is regulated by, this small part of the brain. And this has turned out to be one of the biggest misses in education and training for centuries. Education and training have basically always focused on the moment of epiphany or new understanding. But it turns out that encoding, storing, and retrieving new information require energy, and energy is in short supply in our brains. So, an additional layer, beyond the parts of the brain engaged in having the moment of epiphany, evolved to make a judgment about whether that new understanding would have future value and should be stored in enduring memory or quickly forgotten. And as we eventually uncovered, sometimes, the teaching optimization strategies for gaining an epiphany are in direct conflict with the rules used by the hippocampus to determine whether to store that insight. Let me give you an example. If you are teaching and you ask a learner a question, and they are confident in their answer but also wrong, epiphany-priority focused teaching calls that a “teaching moment,” or sometimes, the “hypercorrection effect.” So, we were all trained to give the answer right away. And while it is true that this has a strong correlation with having the epiphany, it has a negative correlation with the actual creation of enduring memory. It is as if the hippocampus says, “I see that every time I need the answer, it is given to me in real time, so there is no need to spend the energy required to rewire that new knowledge into enduring synaptic memory.” We tested this extensively, and it turns out that if you simply acknowledge that the answer is wrong and move on to another question or two and then come back to the answer that was missed, the hippocampus tends to prioritize this knowledge, as if saying, “I remember missing that; I’d better store it.” How many times have you had an interesting epiphany and only days later could not remember what it was? That is because your hippocampus determined it was not worth storing. Removing Henry’s hippocampus instantly turned off his ability to learn. And as we will explore, that also turned off his ability to have a persistent conscious experience of life. While he was conscious in each moment, without memory creation, he had no persistent sense of his life. This will play back into how we manage memory in AI systems. Scientists studied Henry’s brain for more than fifty years, during which time he lived without the ability to form new memories, and in a final act of generosity, his brain was donated to science after his death in 2008. Researchers at the MIND Institute at UC San Diego performed a painstaking fifty-three-hour procedure to section and preserve it. 10 The entire process was digitally imaged at microscopic resolution, resulting in more than 2,400 slices and a complete three-dimensional reconstruction of his brain. In the deepest irony, the man who could not form new memories became the foundation for how we understand memory itself. The Advent of the Functional fMRI Thirty-eight years after Henry’s original brain surgery, we were given a tool to peer into the brain and advance our understanding of human learning. The year was 1992. At Massachusetts General Hospital, a young researcher named Kenneth Kwong, PhD, was part of a team working on a new imaging technique that used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) not just to take static pictures of the brain’s structure but to watch it work dynamically while interacting. The breakthrough hinged on a surprising fact: When neurons fire, they consume oxygen, and the blood flow in that region increases slightly to compensate. This change in blood oxygenation could be detected using a variant of MRI known as BOLD contrast—blood oxygen level dependent imaging. And with that, the functional MRI (fMRI) was born. Kwong’s paper, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , became a cornerstone in modern neuroscience. 11 It was like Galileo turning his telescope to the stars—only this time, we were looking inward. Also at Harvard, Daniel Schacter, PhD, used the fMRI to explore the architecture of memory and its malfunctions. His acclaimed book The Seven Sins of Memory reframed forgetting not as failure but as adaptation: a system optimized to remember what matters, not everything. 12 In Schacter’s view, when memory distorts or forgets, it isn’t failing—it’s revealing the trade-offs of a system built not for perfect recall but for adaptive reconstruction and forward-looking efficiency, optimized to operate within the constraints of attention, relevance, and cognitive bandwidth. The constraints of having only twenty watts of energy. Meanwhile, at Washington University in St. Louis, Henry “Roddy” Roediger III, PhD, led pioneering studies in retrieval-based learning and memory consolidation, later captured in the acclaimed book Make It Stick . 13 Since 2011, I have had the great honor to benefit from the work of both Schacter and Roediger through their work on the science advisory board of the advanced learning company we built. And memory wasn’t the only frontier. In 2016, researchers using ultra-high-field fMRI revealed how our brains process predictions and reality in layered circuits—with top-down expectations and bottom-up input activating different layers of the visual cortex. We will take a look at this later in our exploration, because it turns out to be core to how artificial intelligence learns and builds its own model of the world. These discoveries hinted at something profound: a hyperefficient layered prediction engine inside the human brain that would become central to AI’s breakout. Their work, and the work of many others, was not just academic curiosity—they provided foundational insights that shaped how we now understand the encoding, storage, and retrieval of knowledge and the efficient prediction-response processing of massive inputs that would help us emerge intelligence beyond biology. The invention of the digital neural network. Moving Our Intelligence Outside of the Constraints of Biology Something remarkable has begun to happen. We are not just studying intelligence. We are building it. As you will come to see, many of the key principles that allowed our biological intelligence to emerge—prediction, feedback, reinforcement, memory updating—are foundational to how modern artificial intelligence systems operate. Miracles of Efficiency As we build AI and discover the intense energy consumption that it requires, the more impressive our per-watt of energy biological intelligence seems. And in some ways, AI is a very clever solution for biological intelligence, for us , to escape the limitation of energy. To plug intelligence into the power grid. And from this perspective, we will explore how we can plug back into AI to benefit directly from that. The miraculous efficiency of our brains isn’t just impressive—it’s an evolutionary necessity. Energy has always been a type of rate-limiting factor for biological intelligence. In the biological world, brains evolved not to be perfect but to make hyperefficient use of a very small amount of available energy. Recognizing this can perhaps help us feel more grounded and less threatened by the accelerating AI revolution. In the pages ahead, we will explore what happens when we take something profound that was developed under extreme energy constraints (biological intelligence) and create a version of intelligence that we can plug into massive energy resources. Desirable Difficulty and the Emergence of Consciousness But before we seek to understand what AI might become, we need to fully grasp what we already are: the conscious intelligence that slowly and magnificently evolved over millions of years under extraordinary constraint, from which artificial intelligence is now rapidly emerging. We will explore how emotional processing, which began in our brains as a survival alert system, was central to the emergence of our own consciousness. We will explore how consciousness arises within the relationship between the brain and the body. And how the introduction of constraints to AI of entering the physical world through robotics may be the key to the emergence of some form of conscious self-awareness in artificial intelligence as well. This isn’t just a technical argument. It is a philosophical one. It invites us to consider intelligence as a kind of elegant emergence—shaped in part by the scarcity of fuel, the delicacy of evolution, the trade-offs of biology. How consciousness itself is a by-product of desirable difficulty. The idea of desirable difficulty is explored in Malcolm Gladwell’s amazing book David and Goliath . 14 At the heart of that book lies the work of Dr. Robert Bjork, who coined the term and pioneered the concept as a foundation of human learning. 15 Gladwell’s book explores how what we often perceive as disadvantages—such as poverty, learning disabilities, or underdog status—can actually create conditions for extraordinary advantage. He argues that real strength can emerge from constraint, adversity, and limitation. 16 The shepherd boy David was not a weaker opponent to the armored Goliath—he was a new kind of opponent, using speed, ingenuity, and asymmetric strategy. Our conversation here echoes this idea that the struggle itself—the “desirable difficulty”—is not a barrier to greatness, but often the very path to it. Through stories ranging from dyslexic CEOs to civil rights activists, Gladwell shows that limitations can produce not just resilience but transformation. Bjork’s work shows that our brains leverage desirable difficulties to learn. His work has deeply impacted my own, as Dr. Bjork has graciously shared his breakthrough insights with our advanced learning company as chair of our brain science advisory board since 2011. Changing How We Think About Learning Just before the Thanksgiving holiday break in 2025, I began to understand the full power of AI in training. It happened as I was testing our new conversational AI training agent that we use to train doctors and nurses on critical topics where mistakes can result in patients dying from medical error. Most people are not aware that the third leading cause of death in America, only behind heart attack and cancer, is death due to medical error. That’s one reason we take our work so seriously at my advanced learning company—we are all patients eventually. The seminal work that disclosed the extent of this critical medical error occurrence at a rate of 268 avoidable deaths per day was called To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System , published in 2000. 17 This report was deeply informed by the work of Dr. Brent James, a towering figure in the world of medical patient safety. Dr. James has chaired my company’s clinical innovation advisory board since 2019. It is important to understand that frontline healthcare workers are heroes who work in the most complex work environment on earth, in my opinion. Imagine a manufacturing line cranking out identical products one after another. Same materials, same process, rinse and repeat. Now imagine healthcare. The challenge is that you are combining the complexity of biology with comorbidity—patients have multiple issues at once, which impact treatment strategies and priorities—and adding distributed round-the-clock decision-making. Add to that, the science of medicine advances at an extraordinary and accelerating pace, making it very difficult to keep up. David Eddy, a key thought leader behind evidenced-based medicine, has said the “complexity of modern medicine exceeds the inherent limitations of the unaided human [expert] mind.” 18 The culmination of years of work was finally upon us as Thanksgiving approached, and I was testing the launch of our conversational AI training agent. I was being trained by my company’s AI training agent on one of the worst killers, sepsis, where an infection triggers a dangerous inflammatory response throughout the body. It is very hard to treat and moves very fast, and if any mistakes are made or delays of only a few hours happen in aggressive treatment steps, the patient probably dies. When sepsis progresses, the body’s inflammatory response causes blood vessels to lose their tone and dilate inappropriately—a dangerous condition called vasoplegia. This causes blood pressure to plummet because the cardiovascular system can no longer maintain adequate pressure to perfuse vital organs. To counteract this, you rapidly infuse crystalloid fluids to restore circulating volume and maintain organ perfusion. However, because the vessels are dilated and their walls become more permeable from inflammation, some of this fluid leaks into surrounding tissues—a harmful side effect that can cause dangerous edema, including in the lungs, putting strain on the heart and respiratory system. If fluids alone can’t maintain adequate blood pressure, you then give vasopressors such as norepinephrine to restore vascular tone and squeeze the dilated vessels back toward normal. But timing is critical: Give vasopressors too late, and organs have already suffered irreversible damage from prolonged hypoperfusion; give them too early without adequate fluid resuscitation, and you’re constricting vessels in a volume-depleted patient, potentially worsening tissue perfusion. Meanwhile, antibiotics must be started within the first hour to attack the underlying infection. In other words, a very complex training topic. I explained my thinking about how to treat the patient and purposefully left off a critical part of the explanation about tissue perfusion to see how the AI training agent would respond. With patience and nuanced focus, it said that my thinking was partly right, then asked how I might think about the missing step. This was unscripted AI performing extremely well under highly complex challenges and getting it right! And here is why that matters. We have known since the 1980s that people trained in one-to-one conversational training by a subject matter expert perform two orders of magnitude better than those trained in a classroom. Said another way, the average person trained in one-to-one conversation with an expert will outperform 98 percent of those trained in a classroom. But after forty years of knowing this, we had no practical way to scale expert one-to-one training beyond nuanced adaptive training models. Until now, because of conversational AI. I believe that in the coming year, you will begin to see the early transition to a time when all human teaching is done in partnership with your personal one-to-one AI trainer. One that knows you well, knows the edges of your knowledge, and meets you there. One that remembers all its prior interactions with you as you learned new things. One that never gets tired or frustrated or has a bad day and will work with you any time and any place you choose. One that is both intelligent and also has some form of persistent memory access to all of its interactions with you. It will even give you observational feedback on what times of day you, as an individual, learn best. It is not hard to imagine that time spent in a classroom is about sharing ideas and discoveries from your newly acquired learning. Teachers become guides to your curiosity and AI trainer explorations, driving topics along a logical path for you to walk along with your AI trainer and discover and report back. There’s a certain poetry to it—the intelligence we are helping to emerge in silicon is now circling back to help amplify the minds that created it. The implications for our education systems, our work life, and our nonwork life are not yet fully understood. And so, we begin. We will explore how our brain’s dynamic learning processes gave rise to storytelling, reason, compassion, and error. And how, once we abandoned a database approach to AI and eventually began to mirror elements of our own intelligence processes, we were able to create a new kind of intelligence. This is where our inquiry begins. Not with fear. Not with awe. But with a sense of quiet astonishment at what we have become within the limits of energy in our brains and a deep curiosity about what happens when we leverage what we have learned from the neural model of our brains into a computer with access to massive amounts of energy. To understand how AI mirrors our intelligence, we must first examine what makes human learning so remarkable from the very beginning. Even before we can speak or reason, our brains are already performing computational learning feats that rival the most sophisticated AI systems. In the next chapter, we’ll explore how those learning feats begin—how the earliest human mind, still preverbal, lays the groundwork for all the intelligence that follows. OceanofPDF.com
